newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Senate leaders warn of spending bill gridlock.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Senate leaders warn of spending bill gridlock.

text.p: Republican and Democratic Senate leaders warned Friday the chamber was headed toward gridlock on must-pass spending bills, with each side blaming the other for the problems.

With just weeks left before Republicans hope to adjourn for the year, Congress has cleared only a handful of the 13-must-pass spending bills needed to keep the government running in fiscal 1997 (October to September). Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott Thursday night pulled a Treasury/ Postal spending bill from debate, complaining Democrats were offering too many amendments to finish work on the measure.

Lott charged Friday that Democrats were playing politics and said he would move quickly to limit debate on amendments to an Interior spending bill now under debate. He also warned Republicans would use other parliamentary tactics to frustrate Democratic amendments. "It will ball this institution up," if Democrats continue their tactics, Lott warned.

Senate Minority Leader Tom Daschle unveiled a $3.1 billion education spending amendment Democrats plan to offer to a Labor/Health and Human Services bill in coming days, warning they could delay the bill or a spending plan that would be needed to keep the government running if they did not prevail.

"This Congress will not leave until we've destroyed the draconian cuts the Republican leadership continues to insist we pass," Daschle said. "If it takes more persuasion, more time, we are willing to do that."

Republican leaders want to pass as many of the nine remaining spending bills as possible. Those that do not clear Congress as stand-alone bills would be folded into a catch-all spending bill to keep the government running.

As part of their effort to force Clinton to accept their balanced budget plan last year, Republicans refused to compromise with Clinton on spending and allowed the government to partially shut down twice.

The government shutdowns were wildly unpopular with voters and Democrats would not mind making Republicans sweat through another round of negotiations on the spending bills in order to remind voters of the Republican tactics last year, aides said.
